invitation: From Concord, London, rural Bengal and Sheffield, across two hundred years. Three of the four read right here in the page; start with the story if you only have ten minutes.

pieces.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
pieces.note: Emerson starts somewhere small and practical, what to buy people at Christmas, and within a page is making claims you will want to argue with. Notice how he builds by aphorism: short, quotable sentences that land like verdicts, with almost no transition between them. It is a useful model for an essay voice that is confident without being long-winded.
pieces.title: Gifts

pieces.author: William Blake
pieces.note: Six quatrains in plain rhyming couplets, nursery-rhyme simple on the surface. Watch how the first stanza is a sly bit of logic, and then the poem abandons argument for a single image that grows and spreads until it fills the rest. Read it aloud and notice how the cheerful metre works against what is being said.
pieces.title: The Human Abstract

pieces.author: Rabindranath Tagore
pieces.note: A young man from Calcutta is posted to a village he finds unbearable, and an orphan girl keeps house for him. Tagore gives the two characters very unequal amounts of interior life; notice who gets the thoughts and who gets only actions and a few lines of speech. The final paragraph steps out of the story into the narrator's own voice, which is worth weighing.
pieces.title: The Postmaster

pieces.author: Pulp (Jarvis Cocker)
pieces.note: A story-song with a named setting, a second character and dialogue, built on what is essentially one chord sequence that keeps accelerating. Listen as a lyricist for the moment the verses stop narrating and start addressing her directly, and for how the arrangement climbs while the melody barely moves.
pieces.title: Common People
